drills.q: Name the two structurally distinct root causes of training-serving skew.
drills.a: Definition drift (two independently-maintained implementations of the 'same' feature) and point-in-time leakage (naive join uses current value instead of the value as-of the label's timestamp).

drills.q: True or false: a feature store fully eliminates training-serving skew once adopted.
drills.a: False -- it fixes definition-level drift by materializing one shared definition into offline and online stores, but doesn't guarantee execution-context equivalence between the batch job and the real-time read path.

drills.q: Which two internal systems first productized the offline/online feature-store pattern?
drills.a: Uber's Michelangelo Palette and Airbnb's Zipline, both mid-2010s.

drills.q: Explain mechanically what pd.merge_asof(..., direction='backward') does differently from a standard merge on entity ID, in a training data pipeline.
drills.a: It performs a time-aware (as-of) join: for each label row it finds the feature row with the latest feature_timestamp that is still <= the label's own timestamp, rather than joining to whatever the feature's current/latest value happens to be regardless of the label's actual event time -- preventing future information from leaking into training.

drills.q: A model's offline AUC is unusually high for the problem domain. What's the first thing to investigate, and how?
drills.a: Suspect point-in-time leakage first. Manually reconstruct a few training examples' true as-of feature values from raw historical data and compare against what the training set's join actually produced -- a mismatch confirms leakage.

drills.q: A team wants to adopt Tecton for a workload that only ever scores in nightly batch jobs. What's wrong with that choice?
drills.a: Tecton's differentiated strength -- real-time/streaming feature computation via a push-based architecture -- is entirely wasted on a batch-only workload; you'd pay its consumption-based pricing for capability the use case never exercises. A simpler batch-oriented store (Feast, or even a warehouse table with point-in-time-correct retrieval) fits better.

drills.q: Design online/offline consistency monitoring for a feature store in production. What specifically gets alerted on, and how do you avoid false positives from normal materialization lag?
drills.a: Continuously sample matched entity/timestamp pairs, comparing the online store's currently served value against the offline store's materialized value, alerting on systematic divergence. Avoid false positives by setting an expected lag tolerance based on the materialization pipeline's actual cadence (e.g. hourly refresh implies some expected short-window mismatch is normal); alert on divergence that persists beyond that window or appears in features with no legitimate lag source.

drills.q: Explain the 'unified execution layer' critique of feature stores and why it argues feature stores don't fully solve skew.
drills.a: Feature stores manage data artifacts (materialized values) but don't control execution -- when training and serving run through different execution contexts (different query planners, timing/retry semantics), even identical feature definitions can produce subtly different results, e.g. differing handling of late-arriving or out-of-order events. The critique argues the deeper fix is collapsing training and serving onto one shared execution engine computing features inline at query time, rather than syncing artifacts between two separate systems.

drills.q: A team needs sub-minute-fresh features for a real-time fraud model but runs an hourly-batch Feast deployment. What's the fix, and what new correctness problem does it introduce?
drills.a: Move the freshness-critical features to a streaming-first computation path (e.g. Tecton's push-based architecture or an equivalent stream processor), possibly keeping batch for features that don't need the freshness -- a mixed architecture. This makes point-in-time correctness harder, not easier: a streaming pipeline needs correct handling of out-of-order/late-arriving events at much tighter timing tolerances than an hourly batch job.

drills.q: Leadership mandates platform-wide feature store adoption citing 'training-serving skew,' including for workloads that are batch-only scoring with no live serving path. What's the pushback?
drills.a: Training-serving skew only exists where there are two separate execution paths (training and real-time serving) computing features independently -- a batch-only workload has exactly one computation path, so there's no skew risk the online/offline split fixes. Recommend scoping the online-store mandate to workloads with an actual real-time serving path, and applying point-in-time-correctness discipline within existing batch pipelines for the rest, rather than paying for unused online-store infrastructure everywhere.

drills.q: Distinguish target leakage from point-in-time leakage with a concrete example of each.
drills.a: Point-in-time leakage: a feature's CURRENT value is joined to a historical label instead of its as-of value (e.g. today's lifetime purchase total joined to a 3-month-old label). Target leakage: a feature is a near-direct proxy for the label itself, e.g. a 'will_cancel' feature computed from data that only exists because the customer already canceled -- this is non-temporal and a point-in-time join won't catch it.
